operationalization: Any part that divides into pieces like itself is uniform by the definition given, and any part that does not is composite, so there is no separate measurement that could confirm or refute the division.
obstacles: The uniform versus composite split is fixed by how the parts are defined, not by a comparative measurement.
rationale: The statement sorts parts by a logical criterion rather than reporting a quantity, a presence, or a comparative pattern. Tissue images and anatomical atlases can illustrate flesh and hands, but they cannot disagree with a rule that labels each part by how it divides. Nothing in a dataset would count as a counterexample without changing the definition.

operationalization: Score each named pair (bone and fish bone, nail and hoof, hand and claw, feather and scale) for shared tissue and developmental origin versus functional resemblance only; shared identity would count against 'only by analogy', and mere functional likeness would count for it.

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape Knowledgebase
candidate_datasets.role: Curated anatomical characters linking vertebrate structures, including bone, scales, feathers, and keratinous appendages, across taxa.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Specimen media for bone, hoof, feather, and scale structure in the named groups.

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: Chicken gene-expression and anatomical context for the developing feather as one side of the feather-scale comparison.

obstacles: Analogy versus sameness has several competing operationalizations.
Fish-bone can be read as spine, fin ray, or bone tissue, and those readings need not agree.
rationale: The examples can be proxied by histology and developmental origin, which Phenoscape and imaging repositories record for some of the structures. Aristotle's own contrast, same versus merely analogous, is not a variable in those sources, and more than one modern criterion would draw the line in a different place. A test can examine the pairs, not decide the classificatory principle as he framed it.

operationalization: Map the gadfly to candidate insect groups with aquatic larvae, then test whether those larvae develop in fresh water and the adult lives on land; a group whose larvae never leave water, or whose adults are aquatic, would refute that reading.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Life-cycle accounts for horse flies and other insects whose larvae live in wet sediment and whose adults are terrestrial.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Dated, georeferenced observations of larvae and adults that can separate aquatic immature stages from terrestrial adults.

obstacles: The Greek oistros is not securely identifiable to one modern genus.
Several insects with aquatic larvae fit a loose reading and would fail a stricter one.
rationale: Life-cycle accounts and observation records can test an aquatic-larva to terrestrial-adult sequence once a taxon is chosen. The name itself is disputed, and different identifications (tabanids versus other mud-dwelling larvae) do not share one life history. Existing data can test particular mappings, not the sentence under every plausible mapping at once.

operationalization: Treat crooked talons as membership in the raptorial orders and gregariousness as checklist counts above a flock threshold in eBird; counts consistently near one would support the claim, and repeated large flocks or colonial roosts would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: Checklist counts for hawks, falcons, vultures, and owls, used as a flock-size measure.

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: Diet and foraging stratum to mark raptorial birds independently of the flock counts.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Species-level morphology and primary lifestyle for the same birds, as context for which species are aerial predators.

obstacles: Gregarious can mean a feeding flock, a roost, or a breeding colony.
Crooked talons are inferred from raptorial orders, which also include species with weaker feet.
rationale: eBird records the count variable directly, and diet tables can restrict the test to birds of prey. The morphological phrase and the social word both need a threshold the text does not give, so the analysis tests a stated proxy rather than a single coded trait. Within that proxy, large vulture or falcon counts would be enough to reject a universal ban on flocks.

operationalization: For each domesticated form in DAD-IS, ask whether IUCN and occurrence-backed taxonomies still list a wild counterpart of the same lineage; a domesticated kind with no wild counterpart, living or historically attested, would refute the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: FAO DAD-IS
candidate_datasets.role: Inventory of domesticated breeds, including horse, cattle, pig, sheep, goat, and dog.

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: Extinction and wild-status assessments for the proposed wild progenitors.

candidate_datasets.name: ASM Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Current species list for wild and domestic mammals, used to keep the name matching explicit.

obstacles: The same kind is ambiguous once domesticates are ranked as separate species.
Several wild progenitors are extinct, so a present-day survey does not match the claim's timeframe one for one.
rationale: Breed inventories and extinction assessments cover the named livestock and many other domesticates. What they do not settle by themselves is whether aurochs and cattle, or wolf and dog, are the same kind, which is the decision the sentence requires. The named examples can be checked; the universal depends on that taxonomic choice and on extinct populations that are not in living-occurrence tables.

operationalization: Code urinary bladder and intestine as present or absent across animals that have a gut or an excretory organ; any species with a urinary bladder and no intestine would refute the implication, and species with an intestine and no bladder would confirm the 'not conversely' clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape Knowledgebase
candidate_datasets.role: Presence and absence of excretory and digestive structures curated from the comparative literature.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Species accounts stating whether a urinary bladder and an intestine are present, including birds and fishes.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: Zebrafish anatomy for intestine and renal structures, keeping the swim bladder separate from a urinary bladder.

obstacles: Bladder presence is not a column in the main life-history tables and has to be compiled.
A swim bladder or other air space can be mistaken for a urinary bladder.
rationale: The implication is a clean presence-absence contrast, and birds are an obvious intestine-without-bladder case already written into species accounts. Coverage across all animals with excretory organs is incomplete in the curated anatomy sources, so the test is solid for vertebrates and thin outside them. A full survey would be a literature compilation rather than a query of one trait matrix.

operationalization: For each phylum, score mechanoreception, vision, hearing, and chemoreception as present or absent; the claim holds if every animal lineage with any sense has mechanoreception and at least one lineage lacks each other sense.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Sensory descriptions for representative animals across phyla, including eyeless and earless species.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: Zebrafish sensory anatomy as a worked vertebrate case with touch, vision, hearing, and smell.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: A phylum-level tree so that gaps in sensory coverage can be counted rather than ignored.

obstacles: Touch is difficult to score in animals without neurons, especially sponges.
No public dataset inventories every sensory modality for every phylum.
rationale: Model-animal anatomy and species accounts can show that vision, hearing, and smell fail to be universal and that mechanoreception is widespread in animals with nervous systems. They do not contain a modality matrix for the whole animal kingdom, and sponges make the word sense itself unstable. The claim is testable on the groups with described sense organs and open at the base of the tree.

operationalization: Map blooded to vertebrates and bloodless to invertebrates, then compare walking-leg number; a vertebrate species with more than four legs would refute the claim, and invertebrates restricted to zero, two, or four legs would weaken the grouping.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Body-plan accounts giving leg number and circulatory type for arthropods and vertebrates.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Vertebrate versus invertebrate placement for the species being counted.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: Leg-bearing marine invertebrates, including crustaceans, with body-size and taxonomic context.

obstacles: Bloodless has to be mapped to the absence of vertebrate blood, and some invertebrates have haemoglobin.
Leg number is not a single open column across phyla.
rationale: Leg number and the vertebrate circulatory plan are standard facts in species accounts, so the main pattern can be checked without new collecting. The Aristotle word does not match a single laboratory variable, because haemoglobin and leg-like appendages occur outside the intended groups. The result is a partial test of a mapped version of the sentence, not a direct query.

operationalization: In staged embryo series, mark whether the embryo arises from a restricted germ region while the rest of the egg is yolk consumed later, and contrast that with insect larvae that reorganize the whole body; a yolk-free embryo using the entire egg as germ, or a grub leaving most of its body unused, would challenge the contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: The Virtual Human Embryo
candidate_datasets.role: Human and comparative early-embryo stages showing the germ disc separate from nutritional reserves.

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: Chicken developmental anatomy, the clearest public series for an embryo sitting on a large yolk.

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: Frog embryonic stages, for an egg in which the nutritional and embryonic regions are less sharply split.

obstacles: Public staging atlases cover chick, frog, and human, not every oviparous group.
The grub side of the contrast needs an insect series that these vertebrate atlases do not contain.
rationale: Chick and frog atlases show the spatial split between embryo and yolk directly, which is the measurable content of the egg half of the claim. Insect metamorphosis, the grub half, is not in those atlases and would have to be added from separate developmental collections. The vertebrate egg can be examined now; the full contrast cannot.

operationalization: Use reproductive mode to split viviparous sharks into internal egg-hatchers and placental live-bearers, and contrast both with horse and human pregnancy; absence of any internally hatching shark, or internally hatching mammals coded like those sharks, would refute the contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Reproductive guild for sharks and rays, including oviparity, yolk-sac viviparity, and placental viviparity.

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: Life-history traits for sharks and rays with reproductive mode as a coded field.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Accounts of human and horse pregnancy as the live-foetus side of the contrast.

obstacles: The shark kind mixes egg-laying, yolk-sac, and placental species.
Internal hatching has to be read from reproductive guild, not from a single column named eggs.
rationale: FishBase and Sharkipedia code the reproductive modes the sentence distinguishes, for most living sharks rather than a handful of case reports. Mammals in the contrast are the standard live-bearing pattern in species accounts. A table join of those fields can confirm or reject the grouping with ordinary cross-tabulation.

operationalization: Compare maximum body length of invertebrate species by habitat (marine, freshwater, terrestrial) and by climate zone of their occurrences; marine or mild-climate lineages no larger than their land and freshwater relatives would refute the two comparisons.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: Maximum length and habitat for marine and freshwater invertebrates.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Georeferenced records used to place those species in warmer or colder climates.

candidate_datasets.name: Copernicus Climate Data Store
candidate_datasets.role: Gridded air temperature used to mark mild versus cold climates for the occurrence coordinates.

obstacles: Bloodless is a wide, non-monophyletic bucket.
Published maximum lengths over-represent large or commercially noticed species.
Mild climate needs a temperature cutoff the text does not give.
rationale: Length, habitat, and climate grids exist and can be joined for a subset of invertebrates, especially marine ones. Sampling favors big, named species, and terrestrial invertebrates are less consistently measured than marine ones. The comparisons are feasible as a biased subset test, not as a balanced survey of every bloodless group.

operationalization: Code hair, including spines, and reproductive mode for living mammals; any hairy egg-layer refutes the universal, and no such species among hairy animals would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Species accounts that state both the coat and whether the animal lays eggs or bears live young, including monotremes and spiny mammals.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote life-history database
candidate_datasets.role: Life-history table for mammals with reproductive traits that separate egg-laying monotremes from viviparous mammals.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: Mammal trait table including the monotremes and the viviparous orders, for body plan and reproduction together.

obstacles: Spines of hedgehogs and porcupines have to be counted as hair, which the claim itself allows.
Extinct hairy egg-layers, if any, are outside the living-trait tables.
rationale: Hair and egg-laying versus live birth are recorded for the living mammals these databases cover, including the monotremes that decide a universal. The scope is essentially the modern mammal list, which PanTHERIA, the amniote life-history table, and species accounts share. A small team can cross-tabulate coat and parity without new anatomical work.

operationalization: On sexed human crania, count suture lines and whether three meet at one point or a single circular suture dominates; a large overlap between male and female patterns would refute the sex rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: Male and female cadaveric heads on which the cranial sutures can be inspected directly.

candidate_datasets.name: The Cancer Imaging Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public head CT collections from which suture patterns can be read in a larger adult sample.

obstacles: Suture pattern is rarely a field in open osteometric downloads.
Series large enough for a sex comparison often remain in museum collections rather than one public table.
rationale: The variables are visible on cranial CT and on the Visible Human heads, so the criterion is concrete. Those public images are a small or clinical sample, not a sex-stratified osteological series built for this question. The pattern can be scored for the available scans; a population estimate of the sex rule would take further compilation.

operationalization: For Mediterranean Talpa and for Spalax, score external eye visibility and whether a pigmented eye remnant lies under the skin, then survey other live-bearing mammals for the same condition; an externally visible functional eye would refute the description, and a second viviparous eyeless lineage would refute the 'only' clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Eye and life-history accounts for moles and blind mole-rats.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: MicroCT and photographs of mole and mole-rat heads showing the orbital region.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Digital morphology of small-mammal skulls as a complement to the eye soft tissues.

obstacles: The animal may be a Talpa mole or a Spalax mole-rat, and their eyes are not the same.
The claim that it is the only viviparous animal without eyes needs a survey beyond one genus.
rationale: Skull imaging and species accounts can test whether a pigmented eye sits under skin in both candidate taxa. They do not remove the name ambiguity, and a different mapping changes how strong the 'cannot see' and 'only' clauses are. The anatomical description is partly testable now; the uniqueness clause needs a wider mammal survey than one genus provides.

operationalization: Compare within-species iris-color variety in humans with other mammals, counting horses separately; several non-human species with stable within-species color polymorphisms would refute 'only or nearly only'.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs in which iris color can be scored for humans, horses, dogs, cats, and other mammals.

candidate_datasets.name: FAO DAD-IS
candidate_datasets.role: Breed standards that record blue or odd eyes in horses, dogs, and other domesticates.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Species accounts that mention eye color when it is unusual.

obstacles: Iris color is not a column in the mammal trait databases.
'Nearly the only' has no numeric cutoff.
Photographs confound lighting, breed bias, and age.
rationale: Breed standards and photographs can show that eye-color variation is not confined to humans, which is enough to pressure the uniqueness claim. There is no curated iris-color matrix, and 'nearly only' can be saved or rejected by moving the threshold. The data support a partial, photo-based test rather than a clean comparative analysis.

operationalization: On head imaging, trace air-filled or patent ducts from the ear cavity: a duct to the nasopharynx supports the palate connection, and an open passage into the cranial cavity would refute the denial of a brain connection.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: Sectioned human heads on which the ear cavity, Eustachian tube, and cranial floor can be followed.

candidate_datasets.name: The Cancer Imaging Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Head CT series showing the temporal bone and nasopharynx in many adults.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Protein Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: Histology of the ear and adjacent tissues as a check on what is a passage rather than a nerve.

obstacles: Passage can mean an air duct or any canal, and those readings disagree.
Imaging coverage is strong for humans and weak for other eared animals.
rationale: Human CT and the Visible Human sections show the middle-ear route toward the nasopharynx and the absence of an air passage into the brain. The same images include nerve canals toward the cranial cavity, so the result depends on whether those count as passages. Other mammals with ears are not in these human collections, so the scope 'animals with ears' is only partly covered.

operationalization: Score voluntary pinna movement as present or absent for humans and for other mammals that have external ears; any non-human species that cannot move its pinnae, or a human pattern of reliable movement, would refute the uniqueness claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Behavioral notes on the external ear for mammals that have pinnae.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs and short observations that sometimes show ear posture changing, as a weak supplement to the accounts.

obstacles: Voluntary ear movement is not a field in trait databases.
Some humans can move the pinna, so the human side is already variable.
rationale: Species accounts occasionally mention mobile ears, but they do not score the ability across mammals, and photo archives were not built for that trait. The comparison is well defined and still lacks a dataset that records it. A test would compile natural-history notes rather than analyze a table, and even then human variation blurs the species-level contrast.

operationalization: For the Nile crocodile and for other jawed vertebrates, score whether the upper jaw, the lower jaw, or both move relative to the braincase during a bite; movement of the crocodile's lower jaw, or upper-jaw movement in another lineage, would refute the two clauses.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Skull models showing the jaw joint and cranial joints of crocodiles, birds, and other vertebrates.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Additional skull reconstructions for the same comparison of joint structure.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Species accounts of how the crocodile jaw and bird or mammal jaws are described as moving.

obstacles: Joint shape does not by itself show which element moves in a living bite.
Kinematic comparisons for birds and fishes are mostly in papers rather than one movement archive.
rationale: Skeletal repositories make the joints inspectable, and species accounts state the familiar crocodile story. Movement is a behavioral variable, and bone shape underdetermines it, especially where birds and some fishes also have mobile upper jaws. Existing skeletal data can frame the test; a decisive kinematic comparison still has to be compiled from scattered studies.

operationalization: Count rib pairs on human torso CTs and on the Visible Human sections; a typical count of eight pairs would support the claim, and a typical count far from eight would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: TotalSegmentator CT dataset
candidate_datasets.role: Segmented human torso CTs in which the ribs are labeled and can be counted.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: Cadaveric sections of the human trunk used as a direct rib count.

candidate_datasets.name: The Cancer Imaging Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Further public chest CT collections for the same count in more adults.

obstacles: Cervical or lumbar ribs occur as uncommon variants, so the test needs a stated typical range.
Clinical CT collections over-represent patients.
rationale: Rib number is a direct anatomical count, and more than one public CT resource labels or displays the human ribcage. The claim is about humans, which is the population those collections sample. A small team can tally pairs and compare the distribution with eight without gathering new scans.

operationalization: Rank brain mass divided by body mass, and separately brain water fraction, across vertebrates; humans outside the top rank on either measure would refute that half of the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Comparative Mammalian Brain Collections
candidate_datasets.role: Brain and body weights for a wide range of mammals, used for a relative-size ranking.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Body mass and longevity context for the same species when a weight is missing from the brain collection.

obstacles: Moistness is not in the comparative brain-size tables.
Relative size can mean a simple ratio or an encephalization residual, and those rank species differently.
rationale: Public brain-and-body weights can test whether humans have the largest brain for their size, under an explicit size correction. Water content of brain tissue is not part of those collections, so the moistest half of the sentence has no matching open table. The size clause is a real comparative test; the moisture clause is not, on current deposits.

operationalization: Score brain tissue for blood, for vessels inside it, and for temperature relative to the body surface; vessels or blood in the tissue refute the first two clauses, and a brain as warm as the body core would refute cold to the touch.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Protein Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: Human brain histology, including vascular markers, as a direct check on blood and vessels in the tissue.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: Gross sections of the human head showing vessels associated with the brain.

candidate_datasets.name: Comparative Mammalian Brain Collections
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative mammal brain sections showing whether a vascular pattern is visible beyond humans.

obstacles: Cold to the touch is not in the anatomical atlases.
Vessels in the meninges have to be separated from vessels inside the brain if the claim is read narrowly.
rationale: Histology and gross anatomy can refute a bloodless, veinless brain in humans and in other mammals represented in the brain collections. Temperature is a third clause and is not in those image sets. Because the sentence is a conjunction, vascular data test part of it cleanly and leave the thermal part open.

operationalization: Count heart cavities and rank them by volume on the right, left, and middle; three cavities with the right largest and the left smallest would support the claim, and a stable count of four, or a different size order, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: Sectioned human hearts in which the chambers can be counted and compared.

candidate_datasets.name: The Cancer Imaging Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Cardiac CT and MRI collections for chamber counts in more people.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative notes on the hearts of other large mammals named in the same discussion, such as the horse.

obstacles: The three cavities may not line up one for one with modern atria and ventricles.
Soft-tissue series are dense for humans and thinner for other large blooded animals.
rationale: Chamber number and relative size are visible in public human heart imaging, and the claim includes man among the animals it describes. A mismatch with three cavities, or with the stated size order, decides the sentence for that core case. Other large mammals are less completely imaged, but they are not required to refute a general count that is supposed to hold for man as well.

operationalization: Rank organs of mammals by blood volume, perfusion, or histological vessel density and see whether the lung is first; another organ ahead of the lung on the chosen measure would refute 'most richly supplied'.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Protein Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: Histology of human lung and other organs for a vessel-density comparison.

candidate_datasets.name: HuBMAP
candidate_datasets.role: Spatial assays of human lung and neighboring organs.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: Gross sections showing how extensively the lung is filled with vessels versus other viscera.

obstacles: Most richly can mean flow, volume, or vessel density, and those rankings need not match.
Quantitative perfusion data are concentrated in humans and a few model mammals.
rationale: Human atlases can compare the lung with other organs on histology and gross blood content, which is the observable content of the sentence. They do not encode one agreed richness metric, and they barely leave humans and model species. The claim is testable as a human and model-mammal proxy, not as a survey of every viviparous lung.

operationalization: Measure the craniocaudal position of the right and left kidneys; the claim is supported if the right sits higher in the animals that have kidneys, and refuted if the left is higher in a large share of that scope, including humans.

candidate_datasets.name: TotalSegmentator CT dataset
candidate_datasets.role: Human CTs with left and right kidney labels, so their relative height can be measured.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: Cadaveric sections of the human abdomen for the same left-right comparison.

candidate_datasets.name: The Cancer Imaging Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Additional abdominal CT series for a larger human sample.

obstacles: The open segmentations are human, so other vertebrates are not in the same table.
Horseshoe or pelvic kidneys have to be set aside as positional anomalies.
rationale: Relative kidney height is a direct measurement on labeled abdominal CTs, and humans fall inside 'all animals that have kidneys'. A systematic human pattern with the left kidney higher would refute the universal as stated. Other species are not needed for that refutation, though they would be needed to test how far any corrected version extends.

operationalization: Count separate cervical vertebrae in lion skeletons; one single neck bone would support the claim, and a series of distinct vertebrae would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Lion skeleton scans and photographs on which the neck vertebrae can be counted.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Further digital skulls and skeletons of large cats for the cervical series.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: The standard vertebral formula for the lion as a check on the specimens.

obstacles: A pathologically fused neck in one specimen would have to be separated from the species condition.
rationale: Cervical count is visible on skeletal media, and lion specimens are the sort of material these repositories hold. The decision criterion is a simple count against one bone. A few normally segmented necks decide the species-level claim without a new dissection series.

operationalization: From accelerometry or direct observation, classify elephant sleep as standing or recumbent; regular sleep while standing would refute the claim, and sleep only while lying on the side would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: Elephant tracking studies, some with accelerometers that can separate recumbent from standing rest.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Behavioral summaries of elephant rest posture.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Opportunistic photographs of resting elephants as a weak supplementary source.

obstacles: Most tracking sets record location rather than lying versus standing.
Published sleep studies cover a small number of elephants.
rationale: Posture during sleep is observable, and a few elephant movement studies have the sensor types that can detect it. The public sample is a handful of animals, not the species at large, and many collars were not deployed for sleep. The claim can be checked for those studied animals and not generalized from a broad open table.

operationalization: Code living ungulates for horns (none, one pair, or more) and for cloven versus solid hooves; a solid-hoofed species with a pair of horns would refute the universal, and the horned majority can be counted directly.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Hoof and horn descriptions for cattle, deer, horses, rhinos, and other ungulates.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Foot and skull specimens showing the hoof and the horn cores.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Published morphological matrices that code hooves and cranial appendages.

obstacles: Horn and hoof type are not columns in the main mammal life-history tables.
Rhino horns and giraffe ossicones need an explicit rule before they are counted as horns.
rationale: The combination the sentence forbids is morphologically clear, and species accounts plus skeletal matrices cover the living ungulates well enough for a compilation. Those characters are not already joined in PanTHERIA-style tables, so the work is harmonizing existing codes rather than downloading one file. Within that compilation the solid-hoof plus paired-horn cell is a sharp test.

operationalization: List horned mammals that shed and regrow the head weapon each year, and record the age at first shedding; any non-deer that sheds, or deer that do not shed after age two, would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Antler and horn accounts for deer, bovids, and the pronghorn, including whether the structure is shed.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Dated photographs of shed antlers and of animals in velvet as evidence of an annual cycle.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Age and maturation fields used when an account gives shedding relative to age.

obstacles: Other cervids, and the pronghorn, also shed headgear, so 'the deer' has to be delimited.
Age at first shedding is mostly in husbandry notes rather than a trait column.
rationale: Shedding versus permanent horns is described for the main families in species accounts and can be checked against photographs of cast antlers. Age two as the onset is a narrower fact and is not a standard coded field. The uniqueness and annual-cycle clauses are partly testable; the age threshold is the weak part.

operationalization: For fox, wolf, marten, and weasel, score whether the penis contains a bone; a bone in each named group would support the claim, and a consistently cartilaginous penis in any of them would refute it for that animal.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Baculum specimens and scans for canids and mustelids.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Species accounts that state whether a baculum is present in these carnivores.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Skeletal media for the same genera when a penile bone has been imaged with the skeleton.

obstacles: Marten and weasel each cover several species.
A bone that ossifies only in adults can be missed in a young specimen.
rationale: The scope is four named carnivore groups, and both specimen repositories and species accounts treat the baculum as an ordinary anatomical fact for them. A small team can check those taxa directly rather than compile a new survey of all mammals. Adult specimens are the right sample, which is a manageable filter.

operationalization: Code mammals for tusks, horns, and interlocking pointed cheek teeth; any species with both tusks and horns, or a saw-toothed species with either, would refute the corresponding ban.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Dental and horn descriptions for carnivores, pigs, elephants, walrus, and horned ungulates.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Character matrices that code tusks, horns, and tooth form together.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Skulls showing the teeth and horn cores for the same comparison.

obstacles: Tusk, horn, and saw-tooth each need a coding rule.
The universal scope is all viviparous quadrupeds, and the characters sit in species accounts rather than one trait file.
rationale: The forbidden combinations are observable on skulls and are already described for the familiar families. Building the cross-tabulation means harmonizing narrative accounts and matrix codings, not running a prepared column. That is a real but partial route: decisive for well-described genera, incomplete for every small mammal.

operationalization: Distinguish deciduous teeth from molars and score which tooth classes are replaced in humans, pigs, and other mammals; replacement of molars would refute the first universal, and any shed pig tooth would refute the pig clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Dental formulas and replacement notes, including elephants and pigs.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Juvenile and adult dentitions in which shed or replacing teeth can be seen.

obstacles: Shedding means replacement of deciduous teeth, not loss of worn teeth in old age.
Tooth-replacement series are not one downloadable table.
rationale: Species accounts record diphyodont replacement and the elephant pattern of molar succession, which are the comparisons that decide these universals. They are narrative and specimen-based rather than a single eruption table. A team can settle the main counterexamples; a complete mammal matrix would take longer to assemble.

operationalization: Measure tooth shade against age in horses and in other mammals, holding diet roughly fixed; darkening with age in horses, or whitening as the general mammalian pattern, would refute the stated contrast.
obstacles: Tooth color by age is not a field in the open trait or veterinary databases.
Diet and staining can mimic an age effect.
rationale: The contrast is measurable, and equine aging guides and small dental series discuss color, but those notes are scattered articles rather than a deposited table. No life-history database records shade. A test requires compiling those series and still has to separate stain from age, so only a weak version of the comparison can be attempted with what is public.

operationalization: Compare male and female dental formulas, not teeth retained into old age, in humans, sheep, goats, and pigs; equal formulas would refute a sex difference, and a higher male count in each species would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Sex-typical dental formulas for humans and the three livestock species.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Male and female skulls of those species on which tooth classes can be counted.

candidate_datasets.name: ASM Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic backbone so that domestic breeds are not split into spurious species mid-count.

obstacles: Counts of teeth present in living adults confound formula with loss and impaction.
Breeds may differ from the species-typical formula.
rationale: The anatomical formula is recorded for these domestic species and can be checked on sexed skulls. Public dental surveys of living people measure remaining teeth, which is a different variable, so they should not be treated as the test. The four species are feasible as a specimen-and-account comparison, not as one sex-stratified download.

operationalization: Join species-typical tooth counts to maximum longevity and test the rank correlation after body size and phylogeny; a flat or negative relationship would refute the rule.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Maximum longevity and adult body mass for the species being compared.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Dental formulas used as the tooth-count side of the join.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: Body mass and life-history covariates that otherwise track both longevity and tooth number.

obstacles: Tooth counts have to be compiled onto the longevity table.
Body size and phylogeny move longevity and tooth number together.
rationale: Longevity is in a dedicated open database, and tooth counts exist in species accounts, so a joined analysis is possible for the mammals those sources share. The join is the work, and the biological confounders are serious: a raw correlation would not distinguish the claimed dental effect from size. The sentence is testable only as a phylogenetically controlled subset.

operationalization: For lizards, crocodiles, turtles, and frogs, score external ears, mammary glands, an intromittent organ, and external testes; presence of any of those structures in the group would refute the corresponding absence.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Accounts of ears, hemipenes or a penis, and reproductive anatomy for reptiles and amphibians.

candidate_datasets.name: AmphibiaWeb
candidate_datasets.role: Species accounts for frogs, including ear and reproductive structures.

candidate_datasets.name: AmphiBIO
candidate_datasets.role: Ecological and reproductive traits for amphibians as a coded complement to the narrative accounts.

obstacles: Frogs, lizards, crocodiles, and turtles do not share one body plan, so the four absences have to be scored separately.
Hemipenes and a crocodile or turtle penis are easy to miss in skeletal datasets.
rationale: Species accounts describe external ears, copulatory organs, and the lack of breasts for these groups, which is enough to test each clause on the main lineages. The four traits are not one matrix, and amphibian tables are stronger on ecology than on genital morphology. The claim is checkable family by family rather than by a single download.

operationalization: From GPS or radio tracks of Nile crocodiles, compare the fraction of daytime versus nighttime locations on land; more time in the water by day, or no day-night difference, would refute the rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: Crocodile tracking studies with timestamps that can be split into day and night and, where habitat is coded, land and water.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Timestamped observations as a rough check on when animals are seen ashore.

obstacles: Only a few Nile crocodile tracking studies are public.
Shoreline error can flip a wet-dry classification.
rationale: Diel habitat is measurable on existing tracks where land and water were distinguished. The public crocodile studies are few and geographically narrow relative to the species. The rule can be tested in those populations and should not be treated as already covered for river crocodiles in general.

operationalization: Pair night-time locations of Nile crocodiles with local air and water temperature; the explanation holds only if they are in the water on nights when the water is warmer than the air, and it fails if they enter water when the air is warmer or if temperature does not track the shift.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: Night locations of tracked crocodiles.

candidate_datasets.name: Copernicus Climate Data Store
candidate_datasets.role: ERA5 air temperature and water-temperature fields for the same nights and places.

obstacles: Gridded temperatures are not the microclimate against the animal's body.
A warmer river does not show that warmth is why the animal entered it.
rationale: Tracks and climate reanalysis can test the temperature fact that the explanation cites, at the scale of river and air rather than the animal's skin. They cannot separate warmth from foraging, safety, or habit as the reason for the move. The thermal clause is partly measurable; the causal 'because' remains confounded.

operationalization: Compare skin color with and without body inflation, holding temperature and background fixed; color change without inflation, or inflation without the stated color shift, would refute the mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Natural-history description of color change in the common chameleon.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs of color states, which do not record whether the body was inflated.

obstacles: The inflation trials sit in papers, not in a deposited experimental table.
Inflation, temperature, and disturbance can occur together, so a dark photograph does not identify the cause.
rationale: The mechanism predicts a specific manipulation, and species accounts plus photographs only document that the animal changes color. They do not pair color with measured inflation. Published experiments exist as papers rather than as an open trial archive, so a reanalysis can use them only by compiling methods and figures, which is a partial route.

operationalization: Proxy 'fly high' with aerial foraging or a high hand-wing index, then score toe count and toe arrangement; a high-flying species with other than four toes would refute the universal, and the wryneck should show two toes forward and two back.

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: Foraging stratum, including aerial foragers, as a proxy for birds that fly high.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Hand-wing index and primary lifestyle as a second flight proxy. Toe counts are not in this table.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Toe arrangements for the wryneck and for representative high-flying birds.

obstacles: Fly high is not a measured flight altitude.
Toe arrangement is not in the open bird-morphology matrices and has to be compiled.
rationale: Flight style is coded, and toe formula is not, so the join is only as good as compiled species accounts. The wryneck clause is a single-species check and is easier than the universal about high fliers. The analysis tests a proxy of the sentence on a subset of birds with described feet.

operationalization: Score fishes for a neck, paired limbs, testes, and mammary glands; testes or mammary tissue, or paired limbs rather than fins, would refute the matching clause, while absence of a tetrapod neck and of breasts would support those clauses.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: Zebrafish anatomy ontology, including testes, kidneys, and fins, and lacking mammary glands.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomy and morphology pages for bony and cartilaginous fishes.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative accounts of fish gonads and the absence of breasts.

obstacles: Neck and limb need definitions that do not make those clauses true by vocabulary.
Zebrafish can refute a universal but is not a survey of every fish.
rationale: Testes and the absence of mammary glands are anatomical entries, not inferences, and a single well-annotated fish with testes refutes 'no testicles at all'. Neck and limb are the unstable words, because fins can be forced into or out of the limb category. The gonad and breast clauses are decidable now; the neck and limb clauses are only partly so.

operationalization: On dolphins, count mammary glands and record whether they open beside the genital slit rather than on the chest; a different count or a thoracic position would refute the anatomical claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Mammary anatomy and live birth for dolphins.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries species directory
candidate_datasets.role: Species pages for dolphins stating live birth and the position of the mammary slits.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: Life-history and morphology notes for delphinids.

obstacles: Dolphin covers several genera that share the same slit pattern.
Whether a slit counts as a teat is a minor coding choice.
rationale: The number and position of the mammary openings are stated in public species accounts for the animals the sentence names. The scope is narrow, so those accounts are adequate rather than a thin proxy. Checking two slits beside the genital opening is a direct reading of existing descriptions and specimens, not a new survey.

operationalization: Score fishes for olfactory organs and for an inner ear or otolith organ, not only for external ear flaps; either organ present refutes the claim that fishes lack both the organs and any passage for hearing and smell.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: Olfactory epithelium and ear structures in the zebrafish anatomical record.

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape Knowledgebase
candidate_datasets.role: Curated presence of olfactory and otic characters across fishes.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Species records, including otolith information linked from fish pages.

obstacles: An organ can be misread as an external opening only, which fishes lack for ears.
A zebrafish counterexample refutes the universal without covering every species.
rationale: Public anatomical databases list olfactory tissue and ear or otolith structures for fishes, which is the opposite of having neither organs nor passages. The universal is decided by those presences even though most species lack a full anatomical annotation. External nostrils and ear openings are a different reading, and the rationale for scoring should keep internal organs in the test because the sentence denies the organs themselves.

operationalization: Cross reproductive mode with bony versus cartilaginous fishes, and check the anglerfish separately; a viviparous scaly fish, or an egg-laying cartilaginous fish, refutes the matching universal, and the anglerfish is scored against the stated exception.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Class and reproductive guild for bony and cartilaginous fishes, including Lophius.

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: Reproductive mode across sharks and rays, the cartilaginous side of the table.

obstacles: Scaly has to be coded so that scaleless bony fishes are not silently dropped or silently included.
The fishing-frog is the anglerfish Lophius, a bony fish, so the exception is not inside the cartilaginous group.
rationale: Reproductive guild and higher taxon are standard fields covering most fishes, which is the stated scope. The two universals can be cross-tabulated directly, and the anglerfish has its own species record. Ordinary database queries are enough to confirm or refute both clauses.

operationalization: Inspect adult cattle and horse hearts for an ossified element; a bone in some ox hearts and in the horse would support the claim, and no such bone in a broad adult sample of either would refute it.
obstacles: The heart bone is a soft-tissue element and is not in skeletal repositories or life-history tables.
It is reported as dependent on age and breed, so a few hearts would not settle the 'not in every ox' clause.
rationale: The observation is anatomically specific and would be settled by a series of hearts, but those series are veterinary papers and teaching collections rather than a public imaging dataset. Skeletal archives do not substitute, because the element is inside the heart. The claim is testable from compiled pathology notes for a few breeds and not from an open download.

operationalization: Score gall-bladder presence in deer, roe, horse, mule, ass, seals, and pigs; a gall bladder in horse or deer would refute those clauses, and universal absence in all pigs would refute the 'some kinds' hedge.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Visceral notes for horses, deer, pigs, and seals, including the gall bladder when the account mentions it.

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape Knowledgebase
candidate_datasets.role: Curated presence or absence of the gall bladder where the literature has been encoded.

obstacles: Gall-bladder presence is not a column in the mammal life-history tables.
Pigs and seals vary by species, so the hedge requires a species-level map.
rationale: The organ is a yes-no anatomical fact, and species accounts plus curated phenotype records cover the named domestic and game mammals unevenly. Mule and ass can be tied to the horse, while seals and the pig exception need species-by-species notes. A compilation can test the list; it is not already a column.

operationalization: In a sample of stags, count dipteran larvae in the retropharyngeal pouch and test whether every animal has a cluster near twenty; any uninfected stag, or a typical count far from twenty, refutes the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Observations of deer nasal-bot flies, which show that the parasite exists but not how many larvae each stag carries.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Host and parasite notes for deer where bots are mentioned.

obstacles: No open dataset gives larval counts in the head across stag populations.
'Without exception' and 'about twenty' are stronger than a presence record.
rationale: Presence of deer bot flies is documentable from observations and host notes. Prevalence and a count near twenty, required by the wording, are not in those sources. Parasitology surveys exist as papers rather than as a maintained prevalence table, so the universal and the number stay only partly approachable.

operationalization: Score kidneys and a urinary bladder in fishes and birds; either organ in either group refutes the universal for that organ.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: Zebrafish kidney records, a direct counterexample class for fishes.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Bird and fish accounts that state the kidney and whether a urinary bladder is present.

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape Knowledgebase
candidate_datasets.role: Curated renal and bladder characters for vertebrates.

obstacles: The urinary bladder must be kept distinct from a swim bladder.
Annotated model species and species accounts refute a universal without listing every species.
rationale: Kidneys of fishes and birds are standard anatomical entries in public databases, so a universal denial is decidable without new dissection. The bladder half is also described, with birds lacking a urinary bladder and possessing kidneys, which splits the two organs. The test is a presence query on existing annotations, not a proxy.

operationalization: For horned mammals that lack upper incisors, count stomach chambers and code cud-chewing; a count other than four, or cud-chewing without that dentition, would challenge the link the sentence draws.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Dentition, horn, stomach, and rumination notes for cattle, sheep, deer, and camelids.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: Diet and taxonomy for the same ungulates, as a frame for which species are horned grazers.

obstacles: Camelids chew the cud with a three-chambered stomach, so four chambers and rumination are not the same trait.
Stomach-chamber counts are in species accounts rather than in PanTHERIA.
rationale: The dental and horn conditions and the stomach layout are described for the main ruminant families. They are not one coded matrix, and camelids show why chamber number and cud-chewing should be scored separately. A family-level compilation can test the rule; it is not a finished download.

operationalization: Count ribs or rib-bearing precloacal vertebrae on snake skeletal CT; a typical count near thirty would support the claim, and counts far above thirty would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Snake microCT volumes on which vertebrae and ribs can be counted.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Additional reptile skeletal reconstructions for the same count.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Vertebral-count notes for representative snakes.

obstacles: The count should be defined on precloacal rib-bearing vertebrae before specimens are compared.
Incomplete tails do not give a whole-body total, but a column already longer than thirty still decides the claim.
rationale: Rib number is a direct count on public snake scans, and the claim states a single number for serpents. Specimens whose visible column already exceeds thirty refute that number even without every species. The analysis is a tally on existing images.

operationalization: Score testes as present or absent in fishes, other gill-bearing animals, and snakes, treating internal male gonads as testes; presence in any of those groups refutes the denial.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: Testis as an anatomical term for zebrafish.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Sex and reproductive records for fishes, the largest gill-bearing group.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Accounts of male gonads in snakes and fishes.

obstacles: The word may have been meant as a compact external testis rather than any male gonad.
Gill-bearing animals include larval amphibians, which should be coded apart from fishes.
rationale: If testes mean male gonads, public anatomy for fishes and snakes already records them and can refute a blanket absence. The alternative reading, external scrotal testes only, should be stated up front because it would make the sentence closer to true by definition. Under the inclusive reading the data decide the claim; under the narrow reading they decide a different one.

operationalization: Record whether testes lie inside the body cavity near the loin in birds, lizards, turtles, crocodiles, and the hedgehog; a scrotal or far-caudal position in any of those groups would refute the claim for that group.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Testis position for birds, reptiles, and the hedgehog.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Soft-tissue or contrast scans when the gonad itself, not only the skeleton, has been imaged.

obstacles: Testis position is seasonal in some birds and mammals and can be mis-scored outside the breeding condition.
The trait is in anatomical accounts rather than a single column.
rationale: Internal testes are described for the named groups in species accounts, so each group can be checked. Season and the exact phrase 'close to the loin' are finer than those accounts usually measure. The test is a compilation across the listed taxa, adequate for the main lineages and not a pre-joined matrix.

operationalization: Compare testis mass or volume just before and during the breeding season across bird species; no enlargement, or enlargement in only some species, would refute the 'all birds' clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Qualitative notes that some birds enlarge the gonads in the breeding season.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: Timing of maturity and reproduction, which does not itself contain testis size.

obstacles: Seasonal testis mass is scattered through papers rather than a compiled open table.
All birds overstates the set of species that have actually been measured.
rationale: The within-year contrast is clear, and many single-species studies have measured it, but they are not a maintained database. Longevity tables do not substitute for gonad size. A team can assemble a literature table for a subset of birds; it cannot download the comparison for every species.

operationalization: Code sharks, dogfish, and rays as internally egg-producing and externally live-bearing, or as egg-laying, or as placental; a large egg-laying share, or no internal egg stage before live birth, would refute the group description.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Reproductive guild for dogfish, other sharks, and rays.

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: Reproductive mode coded across selachians.

obstacles: Skates and some sharks lay egg cases, so selachians are not one mode.
Yolk-sac viviparity and placental viviparity both end in live birth and have to be distinguished.
rationale: The internal-egg then live-birth sequence is what the reproductive-mode fields are for, and they cover the selachians named in the claim. Exceptions are in the same tables, so the universal and the dogfish example can both be counted. This is a direct cross-tabulation.

operationalization: Code snakes as egg-laying or live-bearing and mark vipers separately; any live-bearing non-viper refutes uniqueness, and an egg-laying viper refutes the viper clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Reproductive mode for vipers and for other snakes such as boas and garter snakes.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote life-history database
candidate_datasets.role: Clutch and litter records for reptiles, read with accounts of eggs versus live birth.

obstacles: Viper can mean Vipera or all viperids.
Parity is often in the prose of species accounts rather than a single coded column.
rationale: Live birth versus eggs is known for many snakes in species accounts and life-history compilations. The uniqueness claim is sensitive to how widely viper is drawn and to snakes outside that group that also bear live young. Those cases can be compiled; they are not one filtered field that already isolates vipers.

operationalization: Classify pregnant uteri as cotyledonary or not for horned mammals that lack upper incisors, and for hare, mouse, and bat, and as smooth with a direct attachment for the other toothed live-bearers; cotyledons outside the stated list, or a smooth uterus inside it, would refute the matching clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Comparative Placentation
candidate_datasets.role: Species-by-species placental morphology, including cotyledonary, diffuse, and discoid arrangements.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Dentition and horn state for the same mammals, so the non-ambidental condition can be joined to placental type.

obstacles: Cotyledon is used both for ruminant caruncles and for any knob of attachment, and those must be separated.
Hare, mouse, and bat need an explicit coding because their placentas are often described as discoid.
rationale: A public comparative placentation collection exists specifically to record the uterine attachment types named here, and the dental and horn conditions are in species accounts. The named groups are the scope, not an open-ended sample. With a fixed definition of cotyledon, the presence-absence table can be filled from those sources.

operationalization: Trace the aorta and the vena cava to see whether they connect primarily to the heart or arise from the head; an origin in the head or brain would support the older view the sentence rejects, and connection to the heart with only secondary branches elsewhere would support the sentence.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: Human thoracic sections showing the great vessels leaving and entering the heart.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: Developmental anatomy of the zebrafish heart and axial vessels.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Protein Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: Vascular histology and organ context for the heart and head.

obstacles: Origin can mean the largest connection or the embryonic source.
Developmental series are public for zebrafish and chick, not for every blooded animal.
rationale: Adult human imaging shows the great vessels on the heart rather than sprouting from the brain, which decides the contrast as a gross-anatomical claim. Embryonic origin is a second reading and is available for model species only. The adult connection is testable now; the developmental reading is a partial, model-species test.

operationalization: Count visible heart chambers in small, medium, and large blooded animals under a stated imaging or dissection resolution; three chambers only in the largest animals would support the claim, and four chambers in small species, or three in a small species, would refute the matching clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: Human heart sections, representing a large blooded animal.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: The zebrafish heart, a small species with a known chamber count.

candidate_datasets.name: The Cancer Imaging Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Human cardiac imaging as a larger sample of the large-animal end of the series.

obstacles: Scarcely discernible describes a viewing condition, not only a chamber count.
Public imaging is rich for humans and patchy across a body-size series of other blooded animals.
rationale: Chamber counts exist for humans and for zebrafish, so the numerical half of the sentence can be compared at two ends of the size range. The claim also asserts a visibility gradient, which depends on resolution and is not how these atlases were built. The count is testable; the 'scarcely seen in smaller animals' clause is only partly so.

operationalization: Inspect brain tissue, as distinct from its outer membrane, for blood and for vessels; any vessel or blood inside the brain refutes the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Protein Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: Human brain histology with vascular markers in the tissue.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: Gross brain sections showing internal vessels.

candidate_datasets.name: Comparative Mammalian Brain Collections
candidate_datasets.role: Sections of other mammal brains for the same check beyond humans.

obstacles: Vessels in the meninges have to be separated from vessels in the brain tissue.
A human counterexample refutes the universal without an image of every species.
rationale: The sentence denies blood and vessels inside the brain of every animal. Public histology shows vessels in human brain tissue, and comparative brain collections extend the view to other mammals. That is a direct refutation test of a universal, using atlases that already exist.

operationalization: Map the fibre to fibrin or fibrinogen and compare clotting when that material is present versus removed or genetically absent; clotting without it, or no clotting when it remains, would refute the mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: Mouse Genome Informatics
candidate_datasets.role: Mouse phenotypes for fibrinogen genes, including failure of normal clotting.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Protein Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: Where fibrinogen and related clotting proteins are expressed in human tissues.

obstacles: The removal experiment is in hematology papers more than in a public trial table.
Fibre has to be identified with fibrin or fibrinogen, which is an interpretation.
rationale: Gene-phenotype records capture the prediction that removing the clotting protein stops clot formation, which is the mechanism in modern terms. They are not a deposit of the classical fibre-picking experiment across species. The mapped mechanism can be checked in the mouse and in human protein data; the original manipulation is still a literature compilation.

operationalization: Compare clotting time or clot firmness, and fibrinogen level, in deer, roe, and antelope against other mammals; firm clots or normal fibrinogen would refute the deficiency claim.
obstacles: Comparative clotting times for these ungulates are in scattered papers, not a database.
Weak clotting can mean slow fibrin formation or fast lysis, which are different assays.
rationale: The assay is standard, and hunting and veterinary notes describe unusual cervid blood, but there is no open coagulation table spanning deer, roe, and antelope. Mouse fibrinogen data do not stand in for those species. A test would extract numbers from papers and still has to choose which clotting defect is meant.

operationalization: Score upper-jaw versus lower-jaw movement in the Nile crocodile and in other jawed vertebrates; lower-jaw movement in the crocodile, or upper-jaw movement in any other animal, refutes the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Jaw joints of crocodiles, birds, snakes, and mammals.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Descriptions of jaw movement for the crocodile and for other vertebrates.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Further skulls for the comparative joint anatomy.

obstacles: Skeletal joints do not record which bone moves during a bite.
Cranial kinesis in birds and fishes is documented mainly in papers, not in one motion archive.
rationale: This is the same contrast as the earlier crocodile sentence: specimens show the joints, and movement itself is sparsely archived. Uniqueness fails if any other lineage moves the upper jaw, which requires a kinematic compilation beyond crocodiles. Existing skeletal data support a partial test and do not replace that compilation.

operationalization: Classify the dolphin skeleton as bone or as cartilage like a shark's; cartilage throughout would refute the claim, and a bony skeleton like that of other mammals would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Dolphin skeletons and scans showing ossified vertebrae and limb bones.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Digital morphology of cetacean and fish skeletons for the bone-versus-cartilage contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries species directory
candidate_datasets.role: Species accounts describing dolphins as mammals with a bony skeleton.

obstacles: Fish-spine could mean a different shape of bone rather than cartilage, and that reading should be fixed first.
rationale: Ossification of the dolphin skeleton is visible in public skeletal media and is stated in species accounts. The contrast with shark cartilage is the natural reading of fish-spine here, and those specimens are available too. The check is a direct inspection of existing skeletons.

operationalization: Score horns as solid or hollow, branched or simple, and shed or permanent, and add whether castrated males still shed; another species with solid branched deciduous horns, or intact stags that do not shed, or castrates that shed on the normal schedule, would refute the matching clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Antler versus horn structure and shedding for deer, bovids, and the pronghorn.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Antlers and horn cores showing solid bone versus a horny sheath.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs of cast antlers and of animals in velvet.

obstacles: Castration effects are in husbandry papers, not in a public individual-level dataset.
Solid and branched fits many deer, not a single stag species.
rationale: Structure and annual shedding can be read from accounts and from specimens for living deer and other horned mammals. The castration clause is an intervention result and is not in those databases. Morphology is partly testable now; the castrate exception has to be taken from scattered reports.

operationalization: Score toes and nails or claws across toed tetrapods, with elephants separate; a toed animal without nails, other than the elephant, refutes the universal, and nails on elephant toes refute the exception.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Toe and nail descriptions for elephants, mammals, and other toed vertebrates.

candidate_datasets.name: AmphibiaWeb
candidate_datasets.role: Frog and salamander accounts, for toes that lack nails.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs of elephant feet and of nail-less toed animals.

obstacles: Nail, hoof, and claw need one coding rule.
Elephant toenails are called nails in some descriptions and hooves in others.
rationale: Toe and nail presence is routine in species accounts and is visible in photographs, including the elephant and toed amphibians. That covers the universal and the stated exception without new fieldwork. The remaining task is a consistent label for nail versus hoof, which can be fixed before counting.

operationalization: Code living vertebrates for hair, epidermal scales or scutes, and fish scales, crossed with live birth versus eggs and with feet; hairless live-bearing footed animals, scutes on a live-bearer, or scales on a non-fish would refute the matching clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Integument and parity for mammals, reptiles, and fishes, including pangolins, armadillos, and whales.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Scale condition across bony fishes, including scaleless families.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: Parity and taxonomy for mammals whose coat is reduced.

obstacles: Scale is used for fish scales, pangolin scales, and reptile scales, which are different structures.
Whales are live-bearing and nearly hairless, so hair and viviparity are not the same set.
rationale: Integument and reproductive mode are both described well enough to test the three rules on the main classes. The word scale bundles different tissues, so a careful coding can make a non-fish 'scaled' without matching what the sentence meant. The test is informative once those tissues are separated, and that separation is an interpretation step rather than a column that already exists.

operationalization: Along individual grey hairs, record whether pigment is lost from the tip backward or the shaft is white from the root; a majority of hairs grey only by progressive loss from a pigmented base would refute the claim that most grey hairs are white from the start.
obstacles: Shaft-wise pigment measurements are not in a public human or mammal dataset.
White from the start and greying from the tip are different patterns and have to be counted separately.
rationale: The two patterns are visually distinct and would decide the sentence, but pigment-along-the-shaft data live in dermatology papers rather than in a demographic or trait database. No aging or health survey used here records that gradient. The claim is operational and still lacks a compiled public sample.

operationalization: Estimate baldness rates in boys, women, intact men, and men castrated before puberty, and score post-pubertal body hair in the last group; bald women or early-castrated men, or body hair after early castration, would refute the matching clause.
obstacles: Rates of female pattern hair loss are in clinical papers, not in an open phenotype file I can cite with confidence.
Men castrated before puberty are a historical group with no modern public cohort.
rationale: Baldness in women and age-related baldness in men are widely reported in clinical series, so the universal about women is approachable only by compiling those series. The castration clause depends on a treatment that is not represented in any open cohort. Part of the sentence can be examined through the literature; the pre-pubertal castrate prediction cannot be tested from a current public dataset.

operationalization: Compare juvenile and adult plumage across birds and score the crane's wing from ash to black; any other species with a regular age-related color change would refute uniqueness, and no such change in cranes would refute the crane clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Age-plumage descriptions for cranes, eagles, gulls, and other birds.

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: Age-coded observations and photographs that separate juvenile from adult plumages.

obstacles: Age plumages are described in prose rather than in a coded color column.
The fullest plumage handbooks are not fully open.
rationale: Species accounts and age-coded bird records document juvenile-to-adult color changes in more than one family, which is the uniqueness test. They are not a table of plumage colors by age for every bird. The crane clause and a set of counterexamples can be checked from open accounts; a complete survey of 'no other bird' would need the restricted handbooks as well.

operationalization: Compare lamb color for sires that drank the suspect water before mating with sires that did not, within a breed and coat-color genotype; no shift in lamb color would refute the water effect.

candidate_datasets.name: FAO DAD-IS
candidate_datasets.role: Breed-level coat color for sheep, which records the genetic side of lamb color and not any water treatment of the ram.

obstacles: No dataset records the water a ram drank before mating together with the color of his lambs.
Lamb color tracks coat-color genes, so an unmatched water table cannot identify a water effect.
rationale: The prediction is a paired comparison of water exposure and offspring color inside a genotype. Breed registries record color, and water-chemistry networks exist, but nothing public joins a ram's drinking water to his lambs. Without that join the causal claim cannot be confirmed or refuted from current datasets.

operationalization: In staged series, order the first visible blood against the first differentiated body regions and record whether that blood is inside the heart; blood first in the yolk sac, or a differentiated body before any blood, would refute the stated order.

candidate_datasets.name: The Virtual Human Embryo
candidate_datasets.role: Early human embryonic stages with heart and blood-island timing.

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: Chicken stages, where yolk-sac blood and the heart can be ordered.

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: Frog stages for the same order in an amphibian egg.

obstacles: 'Differentiated as a whole' is a staging judgment, not a single timestamp.
In several model vertebrates the first blood is in the yolk sac rather than inside the heart, so location and order both have to be scored.
rationale: Public staging atlases for human, chick, and frog show heart and blood formation in enough detail to order them. The atlases are model species, not the whole range of blooded animals, and the phrase about the body as a whole needs a stage definition. The order can be tested in those series and not asserted for every embryo from the same files.

operationalization: Code internal and external live birth, hair, and presence of mammary glands and milk for mammals including cetaceans, and the same for fishes and birds; a live-bearing mammal without mammary glands, or milk in a bird or fish, would refute the matching clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: Milk, mammae, and parity for hairy mammals and for dolphins, porpoises, and whales.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote life-history database
candidate_datasets.role: Reproductive mode across mammals, birds, and reptiles.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Fisheries species directory
candidate_datasets.role: Cetacean species pages stating live birth and lactation.

obstacles: Males lack functional mammae, so the claim is about females or about the species.
Sharks that give birth to live young have to be kept out of the internally and externally viviparous class.
